summary: Five of this week's 14 Shorts are new (M1oYlxk9RFI, _Pd72w2dqfc, aEVd7qZEihI, ng1-5nX6YAI, kS3YCq9XsSo). As before, we only have first frames and covers, with no spoken words. The openings that hold put one short line on screen, then one picture that pays it off: a Google search with an absurd answer under 'My bad for asking', or 'AI had enough' above a strange painting (2.86 million views on a 244,000 subscriber channel). Our own 18 reels point the same way, and they count for more than strangers' Shorts: the Maya and Floey duo reels, which say the problem out loud in frame one, get seen and hold attention (12 of 13 passed 100 Instagram views). Saves and shares are still almost zero (5 saves and 2 shares in total).

patterns.name: The voiced frustration
patterns.formula: A character says [the frustration your viewer has] out loud: 'You [did the work] and still can't [know or get the result].' A second voice answers, captioned.
patterns.why: Viewers hear their own complaint come from someone else in the first second, so they stay to see whether it gets answered. This is the structure behind our Maya and Floey duo reels, which are clearly our best at getting seen and holding attention.
patterns.picture: Frame one: Maya mid-sentence and visibly annoyed, with her line as a one-line caption and the problem object (a chart, a page) beside her. Floey's answer gets its own caption by 1.5 seconds, labelled with her name. Use our own characters, never fake posts or quotes.
patterns.forFlowra: You rewrote the page and still can't tell whether it worked.

patterns.ours: Still our strongest result. Of the 13 Maya and Floey duo reels, 12 passed 100 Instagram views and most held people for 7 seconds or more, against 2 to 4 seconds for the garden and pro reels. They almost never get saved or shared (5 saves and 2 shares across all 18 reels), so this pattern wins attention but not saves yet.

patterns.name: The screenshot receipt
patterns.formula: Your [tool or search you trust] shows [the thing, highlighted]. [A character reacts], and here's what it hides.
patterns.why: People read an interface they already know in a split second. The query or highlighted line sets up the joke or the claim, and the answer underneath pays it off before anyone speaks. This week it has the most on-topic evidence: two reposts of the same Google search ('how to get rid of Ai Overview') answered by a staring creature, plus the conflicting AI Overview pair.
patterns.picture: Top: the familiar screen, with the query or one line highlighted. Below: the reaction, either a character or the absurd answer itself, with a short caption. For Floey: the garden's total line dips at the top while she squints at it below, then she zooms down to the one flower that caused the dip. Show only the shape of the line, never a made-up figure.
patterns.forFlowra: Your traffic chart shows the drop. It won't tell you which page caused it.

patterns.name: The fed-up character
patterns.formula: [The thing you rely on, given a face] had enough. [One picture of what it does about it.]
patterns.why: Giving a tool, a judge or a page feelings turns a dry subject into a character the viewer wants to watch, and 'had enough' promises a reaction in the next second. It is new this week from a 244,000 subscriber channel, so the score is not inflated. It is also the layout behind 'Google:' over the brain face. Flowra's pages are already flowers, so this is a natural fit for us.
patterns.picture: Frame one: a one-line caption in a white bar over a dark screen. By 3 seconds, one picture of the character reacting sits under it. For Floey: the caption 'Your oldest page had enough' over a drooping flower turning its petals away from the shiny new ones, while Floey hovers, startled. Keep it to one caption and one picture, with no figures.
patterns.forFlowra: Your oldest page had enough. It lost clicks while you published new ones.

patterns.name: They said
patterns.formula: [The advice everyone in your field repeats], they said. [The deflating result on your own site.]
patterns.why: The first line is a promise the viewer has heard a hundred times, and 'they said' tells them it's about to fail, so they wait for the punchline. The whole joke fits in one caption and one picture. The same 244,000 subscriber channel scored again with the same caption-over-picture layout ('AI had enough').
patterns.picture: Frame one: the 'they said' line alone as a caption on a plain background. By 3 seconds, a single picture of the letdown appears under it. For Floey: the caption 'Just publish more, they said' over a row of shiny new flowers, then the camera pulls back to the older flowers drooping behind them while she stares. Paraphrase common advice only, never an invented quote from a real person.
patterns.forFlowra: Just publish more posts, they said. Your old pages kept losing clicks.

examples.words: On screen: 'Ai will take over world they said' (with a wilted rose emoji). Cover adds the caption 'I'M BRICKED UP'
examples.onScreen: First frame: the caption in a white bar over an almost black screen. Cover: the same caption above a meme picture of a brick wall with loose bricks and the words 'I'M BRICKED UP'. 244,000 subscriber channel

patterns.name: The aftermath first
patterns.formula: Your [page or result] already [took the hit or got the harsh verdict]. Here's [when, where or why] it happened.
patterns.why: When the damage or the verdict comes first, the viewer has to stay for the cause. The peanut Short names the judge ('THE DEVS') and then tells the viewer how to feel. The new bot traffic Short opens on just 'IT' and then 'HAPPENED', announcing the outcome before saying what it is. We borrow the outcome-first structure, never the subject.
patterns.picture: Frame one shows the wreck or the verdict line, or a character holding the bad report, never a calm build-up with no label. For Floey: she lands beside a flower that has already wilted flat, under a caption naming the loss, then rewinds along its stem to the week it started bending. Keep it light, never gory, and show no made-up figures.
patterns.forFlowra: Your best page already lost its clicks. Here is the week it started.

patterns.name: The pinned headline
patterns.formula: A fixed one-line headline naming [the result you want, or a real step count] stays on screen while the speaker says: 'Your [thing] [specific claim]'.
patterns.why: The pinned bar tells a muted viewer what the video is about in frame one and keeps it there, so anyone who joins at second two still knows why to stay. Word-by-word captions under it give the eye something new each beat. The 6,220 subscriber AI Overviews Short keeps climbing (now 24.7).
patterns.picture: A one-line bar at the top or bottom from frame one, with captions building word by word beside a talking face. For Floey: a pinned leaf banner 'Prove your rewrite worked' along the top, while three seed markers light up on the path as she names each step. Use only a count Flowra's process really has: tag the change, wait out the 14 day settling window, compare before and after.
patterns.forFlowra: Check whether your rewrite worked in three steps: tag it, wait, compare.

Cover: the same bar over a stock photo of a young man shouting into a megaphone with a 'Stop' sign. 6,220 subscriber channel. The headline is a yes or no question, so copy the layout, not the wording

patterns.name: Good news with a catch
patterns.formula: Your [gain you wanted] doesn't mean [the result you assume] until you [check the thing you skipped].
patterns.why: It opens on something the viewer already has or wants, then takes it away, so they stay to hear the catch. The Adsterra Short built on 'you have traffic, and it isn't working for you yet' rose from 10.59 to 33.17 this week on a 7,600 subscriber channel. Its first frame has no caption, though, so the hook only lives in the title.
patterns.picture: Something good happening in frame one, with one warning word in a contrasting colour. For Floey: a flower glows under a big AI lens while the nectar line beside it drains. Put the caption on screen from the first frame.
patterns.forFlowra: Your page showing up in AI answers doesn't mean anyone clicked it.

patterns.name: Side by side
patterns.formula: Your [usual view or approach] next to [what it hides], with the second one appearing beside the first.
patterns.why: One thing on screen, then a second beside it, makes the eye compare, and the gap between them is the hook before anyone speaks. The two counters Short is this week's top score (41.92), but it comes from a 158 subscriber channel.
patterns.picture: One panel in frame one, with the second sliding in beside it by 1.5 seconds and a face or character reacting below. For Floey: one flower labelled 'before', then 'after' grows beside it. Show no figures unless they come from a real measured result.
patterns.forFlowra: Your page before and after the change, side by side, adjusted for site movement.

patterns.name: The flat contradiction
patterns.formula: [The thing your field swears by] doesn't [do what you think]. [The overlooked thing] does.
patterns.why: A short, confident claim against what the viewer believes creates an itch that only the explanation can scratch, and it takes under two seconds to say. It works best when the claim and the object it's about share frame one. There is no new evidence this week, so it is kept on earlier examples only.
patterns.picture: One line of large text in frame one, with the object it is about (a search box, a page) right under it. For Floey: she flies past a shiny new flower to a drooping old one as the word 'new' fades out.
patterns.forFlowra: Your next new post won't fix the old pages losing clicks.

patterns.name: Circle the one
patterns.formula: A wide shot of [all your pages or items], then one ring around [the few that cause the problem], with a caption saying what they do.
patterns.why: A crowded wide shot looks like a problem with no handle. Circling one item gives the eye a target, and the caption promises to explain why that one matters. It is new and the closest stranger format to our animated garden. But its score is low (3.77, 11,800 subscribers) and the subject is road traffic, so borrow only the structure.
patterns.picture: Frame one: a tense close-up in warning colour, then by 1.5 seconds a top-down wide shot with one item ringed in a bright colour and a short caption under it. For Floey: a top-down view of the whole garden, then a glowing ring lands around the few drooping flowers while she hovers over them, captioned. This is how the decay queue would look in the garden. Show no counts.
patterns.forFlowra: Out of all your pages, these few are dragging your clicks down.

examples.words: No speech available. Cover caption: 'It opens a gap'. Title: 'One car in 20 shrank a traffic wave. How?'
examples.onScreen: First frame: a 3D animated white car seen from behind in a red-tinted jam under streetlights. Cover: a top-down highway with one white car circled in green and an orange gap opening ahead of it. Off topic (road traffic physics), 11,800 subscriber channel, a 78 second video

avoid: Slow garden openings: an establishing shot, a logo, or Floey flying in. Our garden and pro reels mostly lose viewers at 2 to 4 seconds, while 12 of our 13 Maya and Floey duo reels, which open on the problem said out loud, passed 100 Instagram views and mostly held people for 7 seconds or more. Put the problem on screen and say it in frame one.

Corporate slides with a question as the headline. The answer hubs Short (z65X5U7XMIw) opens on 'How do you build answer hubs that rank in Google AI Overviews?' in blue type on a white slide. The Google AI Mode Short (NTFeqFAIlEs) opens on a grey product slide with a paragraph of body text, and its score comes from a 14 subscriber channel. Use one large line that makes a claim, not a slide that asks something.

Copying yes or no headlines, even when the layout works. 'Is Google Liable?' (KO4LHz0Pwa4) and 'Have website traffic?' (HcWARkOFjDg) let the viewer answer and scroll. Keep the pinned bar but turn it into a specific claim about the viewer's site.

Talking heads with no caption, where the hook is only in the title or on the cover. The Adsterra Short (HcWARkOFjDg) opens on a man mid-gesture with no text, and its only caption ('Wait, you're still here?') comes at the end. It still climbed this week, so this is a judgement call, not a proven loss, but muted viewers get nothing in frame one.

Adding a reaction cam on top of a reposted meme. The same 'My bad for asking' screenshot scored 7.61 on its own (_Pd72w2dqfc) and 4.5 with a streamer stacked above it (aEVd7qZEihI). The face added nothing. Only add a reaction when it is our own character and it says or shows something new.
A calm build-up with no label. The motorbike Short (xbWO6DvxZS0) opens on an ordinary ride and puts 'TOTAL LOSS' only on the cover, which nobody sees in the feed. Name the loss in frame one.

Asking for saves or sends as the hook or the ending. The first save-ask and send-ask reels have produced nothing yet, and across 18 reels we have only 5 saves and 2 shares. It's an early signal, but asking hasn't helped.

Reading a keyword match as topic evidence. The motorbike crash (xbWO6DvxZS0), the helmet-cam vlog (AUZAIx0xuyY) and the traffic wave explainer (kS3YCq9XsSo) matched the word 'traffic' but are about roads. Borrow structure only, never subject.

Leading with a big statistic Flowra can't back. The bot traffic Short (ng1-5nX6YAI) puts '53% of internet traffic is now bots' in its title. Flowra never invents or borrows percentages for hooks, and should name the loss in words, not numbers.

Inventing quotes, posts or testimonials. Complaint posts and 'they said' lines work for strangers, but Flowra never invents customers or user posts. Have Maya or Floey voice the frustration, and keep 'they said' to common advice, never a named person.
Greetings and self-introductions ('Hi, I'm Floey'). Earlier 'Hi!' openings scored among the lowest, and greetings break the house rules.
A mascot who only appears on the cover. Floey or Maya has to be in frame one, reacting to the problem.

Unedited screen recordings as the opening. A plain analytics or tool screen with no caption, face or highlight gives the viewer nothing to look at. The AI Overview Shorts that work show a query and a single answer or highlighted line, with a caption or reaction under it.
Hype numbers and invented counters ('Rank and scale faster', made-up before and after figures). A step count is fine only when Flowra's process really has that many steps.

Calling the before and after comparison a split test or A/B test, or promising indexing. Flowra compares before and after with a 14 day settling window and asks Google to recrawl, but it never guarantees reindexing.
Walls of text and stat collages. Nobody can read that much in the first seconds. Use one line, at most two.
Long tutorial setups (the 78 to 179 second videos). They promise lessons that don't fit a 25 to 45 second reel. Open on the single loss, not the course outline.

Treating the ranking as exact. There are still no spoken openings, and several top scores come from channels with 14 to 158 subscribers (some are likely paid ads). The steadiest evidence comes from the 1,960 to 269,000 subscriber channels and from our own 18 reels.
